response.consequence: Someone who has only a user's email and one backup code can sign in without the password, so a second factor now substitutes for the first. Backup codes are meant to replace the TOTP code, not the password.
response.explanation: In `authorize`, the password is verified only when `user.password && !credentials.totpCode`. The new backup-code branch (`user.twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode`) runs after that check and does not verify the password itself. A request that supplies a non-empty `totpCode` (any junk value) together with a valid `backupCode` skips password verification. The `else if` TOTP branch is not reached either, so `totpCode` is never validated. The backup code alone then authenticates the user. The same non-empty `totpCode` also skips the `ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled` checks. Before this change, a non-empty `totpCode` skipped the password check but still had to pass TOTP validation. The change adds a path where it is skipped and nothing validates `totpCode`.

response.consequence: An attacker who knows only an email can log in to any account that has 2FA disabled by sending an arbitrary totpCode. An attacker holding a single leaked backup code can log in to a 2FA account without the password. Account takeover results.
response.explanation: The password is verified only when `user.password && !credentials.totpCode` (line 121). The third-party provider checks at lines 113 and 117 are also skipped when totpCode is present. Nothing later re-checks the password. The new backup-code branch (lines 131-156) runs when `twoFactorEnabled && credentials.backupCode`. A request with a victim's email, any non-empty totpCode, an empty password and a valid backup code skips the password check and passes the backup-code check. The backup code is then the only factor, and authorize returns the user. If an account has 2FA disabled, `twoFactorEnabled` is false and neither branch (lines 131 and 157) runs. A request with email plus any arbitrary totpCode and no password then reaches the return at line 205 and authenticates. The skip at line 121 is not new, but the new branch makes it worse by letting a backup code replace the TOTP code as the only credential.
response.title: Password check skipped whenever totpCode is supplied; the new backup-code path can then log in without a password

response.explanation: The API client accepts backupCode, the server handles it and returns the new error codes, and BackupCode and TwoFactor register the backupCode and totpCode fields the modal reads. The toggle clears stale values through resetForm. The e2e additions are consistent with the flow.

response.title: No defect in added backupCodes field

response.consequence: A single-use 2FA backup code can be used more than once. An attacker who has a leaked code and the password can open parallel sessions, and a consumed code can be revived by a concurrent login. This weakens the second factor.
response.explanation: The backup-code branch reads `user.backupCodes` in the initial `findUnique`. It then decrypts the list, checks `indexOf`, sets the matching entry to null in memory, and writes the re-encrypted list back with `prisma.user.update`. The update's where clause is only `id: user.id`. It has no transaction, no row lock, and no compare-and-set on the previous `backupCodes` value. Two concurrent logins with the same valid backup code both read the same unconsumed list, both pass the `indexOf` check, and both succeed. Two concurrent logins using different codes each write back a list with only their own code nulled. The later write overwrites the earlier one, so the first code is restored and can be used again.
response.title: Backup code consumption is a non-atomic read-modify-write, so single-use codes can be replayed

response.consequence: A malformed body gives an unhandled exception and a 500 response instead of a clean validation error. Unlimited guesses against the second factor remain possible for a caller holding a session.
response.explanation: The new backup-code branch is entered whenever `req.body.backupCode` is truthy. It then calls `req.body.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` with no type check. A request such as `{"backupCode": 123}`, `{"backupCode": {}}` or `{"backupCode": true}` is truthy but has no `replaceAll`, so it throws a TypeError. The handler has no try/catch, so the client gets a raw 500 instead of a 400 `IncorrectBackupCode`. The branch also reads `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` unguarded. A separate gap is that the endpoint has no rate limiting on password, TOTP or backup-code guesses. That gap existed before this change for password and TOTP, but the new backup-code path adds another guessable factor. I did not find any rate limiting in the visible handler (lines 1-114).
response.title: Non-string backupCode causes an unhandled TypeError (500) in the 2FA disable endpoint
